module.title: Write BFS
goals: write bfs(graph, start) in Python on your own Graph class, using a queue and a visited set, so it returns the vertices in the order BFS visits them

segments.title: Worked example: BFS line by line
segments.body:
Here is the whole function. Each line matches something you did by hand in module 3.

```python
from collections import deque


def bfs(graph, start):
    visited = {start}
    queue = deque([start])
    order = []
    while queue:
        v = queue.popleft()
        order.append(v)
        for n in sorted(graph.adjacency[v]):
            if n not in visited:
                visited.add(n)
                queue.append(n)
    return order
```

| Line | What it does in the trace |
|---|---|
| `visited = {start}` | The start is found straight away. |
| `queue = deque([start])` | The start waits in the queue. |
| `while queue:` | Keep going until no vertex is waiting. |
| `v = queue.popleft()` | Take the vertex at the front. |
| `order.append(v)` | Write it in the order. |
| `for n in sorted(...)` | Look at its neighbours in alphabetical order. |
| `visited.add(n)` + `queue.append(n)` | A new neighbour is marked and joins the back. |

**Running it** on the graph with edges P–Q, P–R and Q–S, starting at P:

| `v` | Order so far | Queue after | Visited |
|---|---|---|---|
| `P` | P | Q, R | P, Q, R |
| `Q` | P, Q | R, S | P, Q, R, S |
| `R` | P, Q, R | S | P, Q, R, S |
| `S` | P, Q, R, S | (empty) | P, Q, R, S |

**Result:** `["P", "Q", "R", "S"]`.
